title: Localizing Validation Messages and Data Annotations
description: Translate built-in and custom validation error messages using resource files, IStringLocalizer, and shared resources across your ASP.NET Core models.

terms.definition: An attribute applied to model properties for validation and display metadata — e.g., [Required], [StringLength], [Range], [EmailAddress], [Display].
A DataAnnotation property that specifies the key of the error message in a resource file, rather than embedding the message directly in code.
The type of the resource class that contains the localized error message. Used alongside ErrorMessageResourceName.
A common resource file (SharedResource.resx) accessible from any model, controller, or view in the app — avoids duplicating the same strings.
A service that creates IStringLocalizer instances for types that are not directly associated with a resource file — used with shared resources.

data.text: When a user submits an invalid form, they see the error message in the language of your app. If your app supports French and Spanish users, those users should see validation errors in their language too — not just your UI labels and buttons.
There are three main approaches to localizing validation messages, ordered from simplest to most flexible:

data.title: Three approaches to validation localization
items: Hardcoded string keys resolved by AddDataAnnotationsLocalization — simplest for small apps.
ErrorMessageResourceName / ErrorMessageResourceType pointing to a class resource file — strongly typed.
Custom ValidationAttribute with IStringLocalizer injected at runtime — most flexible.

data.text: The easiest path is to keep your ErrorMessage strings in English in the model, then create resource files with matching keys. `AddDataAnnotationsLocalization()` handles the lookup automatically:

data.title: Models/Product.cs — model with localized-ready error messages
data.content: ErrorMessage strings serve as keys that must match entries in the resource file exactly.

data.title: Resources/Models/Product.fr.resx — French error messages
data.content: Each data name matches the English ErrorMessage string exactly. The value is the French translation.
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<root>
  <data name="Product name is required" xml:space="preserve">
    <value>Le nom du produit est obligatoire</value>
  </data>
  <data name="Product name must be under 100 characters" xml:space="preserve">
    <value>Le nom du produit ne peut pas dépasser 100 caractères</value>
  </data>
  <data name="Price must be between {0} and {1}" xml:space="preserve">
    <value>Le prix doit être compris entre {0} et {1}</value>
  </data>
  <data name="Invalid supplier email address" xml:space="preserve">
    <value>Adresse e-mail du fournisseur invalide</value>
  </data>
</root>

data.title: Key matching is exact and case-sensitive
data.text: The resource file key must match the ErrorMessage string character for character. If there's even a trailing space mismatch, ASP.NET Core won't find the translation and will fall back to the hardcoded English message.
If multiple models share common validation messages (like 'This field is required'), a shared resource file avoids duplication:

data.title: Resources/SharedResource.resx — shared English strings
data.content: A resource file not tied to any specific class — accessible from anywhere via IStringLocalizerFactory.
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<root>
  <data name="RequiredField" xml:space="preserve">
    <value>This field is required</value>
  </data>
  <data name="InvalidEmail" xml:space="preserve">
    <value>Please enter a valid email address</value>
  </data>
  <data name="MaxLengthExceeded" xml:space="preserve">
    <value>This field cannot exceed {0} characters</value>
  </data>
</root>

data.title: Resources/SharedResource.fr.resx — shared French strings
data.content: French translations for the same shared keys.
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<root>
  <data name="RequiredField" xml:space="preserve">
    <value>Ce champ est obligatoire</value>
  </data>
  <data name="InvalidEmail" xml:space="preserve">
    <value>Veuillez saisir une adresse e-mail valide</value>
  </data>
  <data name="MaxLengthExceeded" xml:space="preserve">
    <value>Ce champ ne peut pas dépasser {0} caractères</value>
  </data>
</root>

data.title: Using SharedResource in a custom validation attribute
data.content: Inject IStringLocalizer<SharedResource> into a custom ValidationAttribute to pull shared, localized error messages.

data.text: For strongly typed access to resource messages, use `ErrorMessageResourceName` (the key) and `ErrorMessageResourceType` (the resource class). This approach works with auto-generated resource classes:

data.title: Models/Customer.cs — strongly typed resource references
data.content: ErrorMessageResourceType points to the auto-generated resource class for the .resx file.

data.title: Resource class generation
data.text: When you add a .resx file to your project, Visual Studio generates a strongly-typed class (e.g., ValidationMessages) with a property for each resource key. The class is in the same namespace as the .resx file.
Built-in attributes like [Required] and [EmailAddress] show English messages by default. To localize them, create a resource file and configure it via `AddDataAnnotationsLocalization`:

data.title: Program.cs — register data annotations localization
data.content: Call AddDataAnnotationsLocalization and optionally point it to a shared resource location.

data.title: Resources/DataAnnotations.fr.resx — French built-in messages
data.content: Keys are the default English messages; values are French translations.
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<root>
  <!-- Required attribute default message -->
  <data name="The {0} field is required." xml:space="preserve">
    <value>Le champ {0} est obligatoire.</value>
  </data>
  <!-- StringLength default message -->
  <data name="The field {0} must be a string with a maximum length of {1}." xml:space="preserve">
    <value>Le champ {0} doit être une chaîne de {1} caractères maximum.</value>
  </data>
  <!-- Range default message -->
  <data name="The field {0} must be between {1} and {2}." xml:space="preserve">
    <value>Le champ {0} doit être compris entre {1} et {2}.</value>
  </data>
  <!-- EmailAddress default message -->
  <data name="The {0} field is not a valid e-mail address." xml:space="preserve">
    <value>Le champ {0} n'est pas une adresse e-mail valide.</value>
  </data>
</root>

data.text: Custom Validation Attribute with Localized Messages

The most flexible approach is a custom ValidationAttribute that uses `IStringLocalizer` to look up messages at runtime. This keeps all error text in resource files, making it easy for translators to update:

data.title: Validation/FutureDateAttribute.cs
data.content: A custom validation attribute that checks a date is in the future, with localized error messages from a resource file.

data.title: Resources/Validation/FutureDateAttribute.fr.resx
data.content: French translation for the custom validation error message.
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<root>
  <data name="DateCannotBeInFuture" xml:space="preserve">
    <value>La date ne peut pas être dans le futur</value>
  </data>
</root>

data.title: Using the custom attribute in a model
data.content: The attribute name is all you write in the model — the error message comes from the resource file.

data.text: A common localization bug is missing keys in a secondary resource file. When ASP.NET Core can't find a translation, it silently falls back to the default language — which can be confusing for users and developers alike.

data.title: Missing key behavior
data.text: If the French resource file doesn't contain the key 'Product name is required', ASP.NET Core silently uses the English ErrorMessage string. Always verify that all resource files contain the same set of keys.

data.caption: How ASP.NET Core resolves a localized validation error message
data.definition:
flowchart LR
    A[User submits form] --> B[Model Validation runs]
    B --> C{[Required] on Name fires]
    C --> D[Look for key in Product.fr.resx]
    D -->|found| E[Return French message]
    D -->|missing| F[Fall back to ErrorMessage string]
    E --> G[Display in French]
    F --> H[Display in English (fallback)]

data.title: Exercise: Localize an Order Model
data.description: Apply all three validation localization approaches to an Order model.
steps: Create an Order model with [Required], [Range], [EmailAddress], and [StringLength] on CustomerName, TotalAmount, CustomerEmail, and ShippingAddress.
Use Approach 1 (AddDataAnnotationsLocalization) for [Required] messages with ErrorMessage strings as keys.
Create Resources/Models/Order.fr.resx and Order.es.resx with French and Spanish translations for each ErrorMessage key.
Add a custom [FutureOrderDate] validation attribute that uses IStringLocalizer<FutureOrderAttribute> for its error message.
Run the app, submit an empty form, and verify the error messages appear in French when ?culture=fr-FR is set.
data.expectedOutcome: An Order form where every validation error message appears in the user's selected language, including messages from the custom validation attribute.

items.text: Every ErrorMessage string has a matching key in all culture resource files

items.hint: Never hardcode error messages in custom attributes

items.text: SharedResource.resx contains strings used across multiple models
items.hint: Avoids duplicating 'This field is required' everywhere

items.text: Resource file placement matches the expected convention
All cultures show the same set of keys — no missing translations

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: AddDataAnnotationsLocalization() enables automatic translation of DataAnnotation error messages.
The ErrorMessage string is the resource key — it must match exactly across all .resx files.
Use ErrorMessageResourceName + ErrorMessageResourceType for strongly-typed resource access.
SharedResource.resx stores common strings used by multiple models and custom attributes.
Custom ValidationAttributes should inject IStringLocalizer via context.GetService<IStringLocalizer<T>>() — never hardcode error messages.
Always verify all resource files contain the same set of keys to avoid silent fallback to English.
data.takeaway: Well-localized validation messages make your app feel truly native to each language. They are the detail users notice most when switching languages.

items.question: Do I need ErrorMessageResourceType for every attribute?
items.answer: No. Use ErrorMessageResourceType only if you want strongly-typed access to a specific resource class. For most cases, AddDataAnnotationsLocalization with matching keys in a per-model .resx file is simpler.

items.question: What if a resource key is missing from the French file?
items.answer: ASP.NET Core silently falls back to the ErrorMessage string (English). This is why resource completeness checks are essential — you won't see an error, just untranslated text.

items.question: Can I use a PO file instead of .resx for validation messages?
items.answer: Yes. If you have AddPortableObjectLocalization() registered, DataAnnotation messages will also be looked up in PO files using the same key-matching approach.

items.question: How do I localize the [Display(Name = "...")] attribute?
items.answer: Add a resource file for the model. For a Product model, create Product.resx, Product.fr.resx, Product.es.resx with keys matching the Name values. ASP.NET Core looks them up automatically when AddDataAnnotationsLocalization() is registered.
